Physics of Language Models: Part 3.2, Knowledge Manipulation

A controlled synthetic experiment in which the authors control every fact a model is pretrained on: language models retrieve stored facts near-perfectly, but classifying or comparing those same facts needs chain-of-thought at both training and inference, and inverse search — recovering the person from an attribute — stays under 2% in every ordinary configuration tested.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

GPT-4 can often answer "Did Aristotle use a laptop?" or "Would a pear sink in water?" — StrategyQA's implicit-reasoning questions — correctly. But that success is confounded two ways at once: maybe the model saw an equivalent statement during pretraining (so it's retrieval dressed up as reasoning), or maybe it genuinely reasons over stored facts but the benchmark can't isolate that from everything else a huge web corpus contains. Prior work on whether language models can manipulate their stored knowledge — take two facts it already knows and combine them into an answer it was never shown — has always run into this same wall: with internet-scale pretraining data, there is no clean way to know what the model was and wasn't exposed to in some paraphrased form.

This paper's fix is to build the pretraining data itself. The authors generate a synthetic biography corpus for up to 100,000 fictitious individuals, each with six independent attributes (birth date, birth city, university, major, employer, employer city), and control exactly which sentences the model sees. That lets them establish — not assume — that an attribute is perfectly stored: they can directly measure that a model extracts a person's birth date or major with close to 100% accuracy, then ask a categorically different question: can the same model, having stored that fact essentially perfectly, use it to answer "was this person born in an even month?" or "who was born on this date, in this city?" — questions it was fine-tuned on for other people in the dataset but never for this specific held-out person.

The comparison with the previous paper in this survey is instructive. Wei et al.'s sycophancy study establishes "the model knows the statement is wrong but says otherwise anyway" purely behaviorally — by watching outputs change under social pressure, with no independent evidence the model actually holds the correct belief internally. Here, "the model knows it" is established by construction: the authors wrote the pretraining data, so per-attribute extraction accuracy is a direct, checkable measurement, not an inference from behavior. That is a strictly stronger form of evidence for the storage half of the argument — though, as the critique below covers, it is stronger specifically in this synthetic setting, and carrying that certainty over to a production model trained on the real internet is a separate step the paper does not get to take for free.

// how it works

The method

The paper studies four task families, each phrased as a question about a fictitious person's stored attributes: retrieval ("What is A's attribute X?"), classification ("Is A's attribute X even or odd?", or its value mod some p), comparison ("Is A greater than B in attribute X?", both a Yes/No ranking version and a numeric-subtraction version), and inverse search ("Which person has attribute X equal to T?"). Figure 1 lays out exactly what counts as "knowledge manipulation" in scope for this paper (path A: the model infers the answer from a function of knowledge it saw during pretraining) versus three adjacent cases that are explicitly out of scope — the model not knowing the fact at all (studied in the companion Part 3.1 paper), the model having seen an equivalent question verbatim (memorization, not manipulation), and the model not understanding the operator itself (e.g., not knowing what "even" means).

The experimental protocol splits the 100,000 synthetic individuals into a training half and a held-out test half, Ptest. Every individual's biography (the six-attribute paragraph) is in the pretraining data for both halves, so extraction ability is uniform across the split by construction. The model is then fine-tuned (via LoRA) on manipulation QA pairs for the training half only, and evaluated on out-of-distribution generalization to the QA pairs for Ptest individuals — people whose biography the model has memorized but whose classification/comparison/inverse-search answer it has never seen. This is what separates "manipulation ability" from ordinary in-distribution fine-tuning: a model that memorizes training-set QA pairs directly would still fail Ptest if it hadn't actually learned the underlying operation.

To test the chain-of-thought hypothesis, the authors define two fine-tuning regimes. In "train without hint," the model only ever sees direct question→answer pairs. In "train with hint," 50% of training examples additionally spell out the relevant attribute before the answer (e.g., "…October; September. No." for a birth-month comparison) — teaching the model, if it can learn to use it, to generate its own chain-of-thought before answering. At test time a model trained without hints is only ever tested without one; a model trained with hints is tested both ways. That is what lets Figure 4 report, per model, one test acc column for "trained w/o hint," then three columns for "trained with hint" — test acc (with hint), test acc (w/o hint), and hint acc, the last measuring whether the model's self-generated hint is itself correct — three of the four {trained}×{tested} combinations side by side, with the fourth ({trained w/o hint} × {tested with hint}) never run.

The models pretrained on bioS multi5+permute — five diversely-phrased, randomly-permuted biographical entries per person — are the ones used as the base for Results 3–6: per Figure 3's own data for that exact configuration, they extract birth dates at 100% and majors at 97.7% accuracy on held-out individuals, matching the paper's stated "nearly 100% … and 98% for majors." That is the empirical anchor for "perfectly stored" — not a qualitative gesture, but a specific, checkable extraction number on the exact model used downstream.

// what they found

The results

Retrieval is easy — once the data is augmented, and except for one thing

Result 1 (Figure 3, middle block) shows dual-attribute retrieval — answering two attributes in one response, e.g. "which company did A work for and where" — is nearly perfect once the pretraining data is sufficiently diversified: for bioS multi5+permute, every dual-retrieval column scores 90–100%, against a baseline of essentially 0%. But order matters when the two attributes have a fixed spatial relationship in the source text: for bioS multi5+fullname, where the company name always precedes the company city in every training sentence, asking for company-then-city (94.9%) is dramatically easier than city-then-company (17.4%) — retrieving in the pretraining order works, retrieving against it collapses.

Result 2 (Figure 3, left block) is sharper: even a perfectly-extractable attribute can fail when only part of it is requested. A model that nails "what is A's birth date" (100% on QA bdate for the best-augmented configuration) can still fail "what is A's birth year" — the QA byear column falls to just 20.4% for that same row, the one column where the otherwise near-perfect bioS multi5+permute configuration collapses. The authors read both results as early evidence that the model needs to explicitly generate the full attribute (month, day, year, in that trained order) before it can extract a sub-piece — it can't "skip ahead" to a later token.

Classification and comparison need CoT — during training and inference

Results 3–5 use models that are already near-perfect extractors (100%/97.7% for birth date/major, per above) and ask them to classify or compare. Without any hint training, accuracy climbs slowly and stays well under the with-hint ceiling: classifying birth-month parity needs 10,000 training examples to reach 75.9% (the paper's "10,000 samples for 75% accuracy," Result 3), and ranking two birth months needs 50,000 examples to reach 85.6% — both far more than the O(12) and O(12²) sample complexity the tasks should need in theory, since the model already knows every birth month perfectly.

Comparing 100 possible majors is the sharpest example, and it is worth being precise about which specific sub-task stays flat: Figure 13's own caption states that major subtraction — "how much luckier is A's major than B's" — "cannot be performed better than random guessing even after providing 2.5 million fine-tuning examples" (1.0% → 1.2% w/o-hint accuracy from 50k to 2.5M training examples, against a 1.0% baseline). Major ranking ("is A's major luckier than B's," Yes/No) does improve substantially over the same range — 50.5% baseline to 69.7% at 2.5M examples w/o hint — a real if incomplete gain, not a flat line. Both facts come from the same figure (Figure 13); the main-text bullet list's shorthand ("ranking 100 majors barely outperforms random") is more precise as a statement about subtraction specifically.

Training with hints doesn't rescue the no-hint pathway (Result 4): at 10,000 birth-month-classification examples, a model trained entirely without hints reaches 75.9% tested without a hint; a model trained with 50%-hinted data and then tested without a hint reaches only 80.3% — barely better, despite having seen chain-of-thought during training. The same hint-trained model tested with its hint reaches 94.2%, and its self-generated hint is itself correct 91.0% of the time (which is consistent with the paper's own footnote-14 arithmetic: 91.0% + (1 − 91.0%) × 50% ≈ 95.5%, close to the observed 94.2%). So hint training buys a large gain only when the hint is actually used at test time — it does not meaningfully improve the no-hint pathway itself. And fine-tuning first for pure knowledge extraction doesn't transfer to manipulation either (Result 5): the BIO-pretrained and QA-finetuned columns in Figure 4 track each other closely task by task, rather than the QA-finetuned (extraction-practiced) model pulling ahead.

Inverse search: under 2%, in every ordinary configuration

Result 7 is the paper's starkest number. Across all 16 ordinary (non-reversed) pretraining configurations tested — every combination of bioS single/multi2/multi5 with permutation and full-name variants — and all 20 inverse-search question variants (asking for the first name only, or the full name; from one attribute, or from a combination of up to four), every one of the 320 resulting cells falls at or below 1.7%, against a similarly near-zero baseline — and the columns asking for the full name (rather than just the first name) score exactly 0.0% in all 16 rows. Accuracy recovers sharply — to 90%+ on some column groups — only in four control rows where the biography text is literally rewritten so an attribute appears before the person's name in the source document. As the paper is careful to note, once the order is truly reversed in pretraining, "the task is no longer inverse knowledge search" — these rows are a positive control confirming the mechanism, not evidence against the near-zero result.

The paper's own explanation (§5, footnote 17) attributes this specifically to the left-to-right autoregressive factorization: if the model learns "A equals B" it cannot infer "B equals A" unless that direction is also in the training data, "period." It explicitly pre-empts the obvious counter — a bidirectional model like BERT — by citing the companion Part 3.1 paper's finding that BERT-style masked-LM pretraining already struggles with plain (forward) extraction, so bidirectionality is not a free fix.

Grounding it in production models

Results 6 and 8 check whether real, already-deployed models show the same pattern qualitatively. On ~4,779 Wikipedia biographies (Figure 5), GPT-4 retrieves birthday+year at 99% but classifying birth-month parity lands at 50.7% correct — indistinguishable from a coin flip — and ranking two birth dates by earlier/later swings from 52.3% (celebrities born 1900–1910, near-chance) up to 81.6% (all pairs), tracking how much of that era's data GPT-4 likely saw. On the inverse-search side (Figure 7), GPT-4 predicts the next sentence of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice at 65.9% but the preceding sentence at only 0.8% — and the same forward/inverse gap repeats across five more Austen novels, a Wikipedia-bio inverse-lookup task (23.9%/42% inverse vs. 89.5%/99% forward for GPT-3.5/GPT-4), and two Chinese-language tasks (idiom letter-infilling and classical poetry line-recall), with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 both showing the same direction every time — 12 of 12 paired cells in the Austen task alone.

Result 9 proposes three mitigations, with different levels of evidence behind each in this paper: rewriting pretraining data to include reversed knowledge is quantitatively evaluated here (the reversed rows of Figure 6, recovering to 90%+ on matching column groups) and handed off to a dedicated follow-up paper the authors also co-authored; retrieval-augmented generation is cited to prior work, not tested in this paper; and inserting document line numbers — illustrated with a single Bible passage where GPT-4 uses chapter/verse numbers as an explicit counting aid — is a qualitative example, not a measured accuracy result.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The controlled-pretraining design is genuinely the paper's strength, and it delivers on what it promises: within the synthetic setting, "perfectly stored, still unusable" is not an inference from behavior but a directly measured gap between two accuracy numbers on the same model. The question worth pressing is how far the word "inherent" in the abstract is entitled to travel from that setting.

v2 adds GPT-2/Llama/Mistral replications of the same synthetic experiments (Figures 10, 12, 13) — that's evidence the result isn't a GPT-2 architecture artifact, which is valuable, but it's still evidence gathered entirely inside the controlled synthetic corpus. The separate claim that this generalizes to models trained on the real internet rests on Figures 2, 5, 7, 9, and 15 — GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama-3 failing similarly on Wikipedia biographies, Jane Austen novels, Chinese idioms, and classical poetry. That evidence is real and consistent (every paired forward/inverse comparison in Figure 7 points the same direction), but the paper is explicit that it is not controlled in the way the synthetic experiment is: "it remains unclear if GPT-4 has seen [these questions] during its pretraining" (p.11). So the strongest, most certain form of the claim — perfectly-stored-yet-unmanipulable — is established for controlled synthetic biographies across three architectures; its extension to production LLMs on real corpora is corroborated but not itself controlled, and the paper says so.

A second, more specific point: the headline claim that CoT must be used "during both training and inference" is tested in the synthetic setting via exactly two fine-tuning regimes — "trained without hint," tested only without a hint at inference, and "trained with hint," evaluated both with and without a hint at test time (per the paper's own footnote 9) — and nothing in between. There is no synthetic ablation for a model fine-tuned without any hint data that is then simply prompted with a CoT instruction at inference time only, with no gradient update. That's a real gap, because the real-world GPT-4 examples in Figures 2, 9 and 15 are exactly that condition — a production model the authors never fine-tuned, unlocked purely by an inference-time prompt asking it to state the attribute before answering. Those examples show inference-time-only CoT working on GPT-4; the controlled experiment that would show whether it works on the paper's own fine-tuned checkpoints is the one condition Figure 4 doesn't include.

On the synthetic-vs-real-knowledge-uniformity question, the paper is more self-aware than a first read suggests: Figure 8's Bible example — GPT-4 successfully performing inverse search on Bible verses via CoT — is explained by the fact that "the Bible is 'sufficiently augmented' on the internet data, chapter/verse numbers appear both before and after," i.e. real text is not uniformly forward-only the way an unmodified synthetic biography is, and the authors use that unevenness to explain why some real-world inverse-search tasks (Bible, apparently) might do better than others (Jane Austen, empirically much worse) rather than treating it as a threat to the synthetic result.

baselines

Every result is reported against an explicit random-guess baseline printed in the same figure (50.0% for binary classification, 54.2%/50.5% for the two ranking tasks, 1.0%/3.6%/8.3% for subtraction and higher-modulus classification) — the right choice for a controlled study with no external "SOTA model" to compare against.

contamination

Designed out by construction for the synthetic experiments — every biography is invented and Ptest QA pairs are held out of fine-tuning. The real-world GPT-4/GPT-3.5 checks carry the opposite risk (can't rule out the model having seen an equivalent phrasing), which the paper flags itself rather than glossing over.

what's missed

An inference-time-only-CoT ablation on the paper's own fine-tuned checkpoints (as opposed to on a production GPT-4 the authors didn't train) — the one condition between "trained without hint" and "trained with hint" that Figure 4 doesn't test.

would raise confidence

That missing ablation, plus a systematic (many-document, not single-Bible-passage) evaluation of the line-numbering mitigation Result 9 proposes but only illustrates qualitatively.

// bottom line

The core finding survives close reading of its own figures: retrieval near-100%, classification/comparison stuck below the with-hint ceiling absent CoT at both training and test time, inverse search under 2% outside of literal-reversal controls. The one place the paper's own prose is looser than its own data is which specific comparison task "barely outperforms random" at 2.5M samples — it's major subtraction (1.0%→1.2%), not major ranking (50.5%→69.7%) — a precision slip in a bullet list, not a hole in the underlying result.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Perfect storage does not imply usable knowledge: the same model that extracts birth dates at 100% and majors at 97.7% classifies birth-month parity at chance-adjacent rates without chain-of-thought, and needs 10,000–50,000 fine-tuning examples just to beat theory-predicted sample complexity by orders of magnitude.
  2. Chain-of-thought has to be present at both training and inference for these tasks — training with hints doesn't rescue no-hint test accuracy, and knowledge-extraction fine-tuning doesn't transfer to manipulation. The one comparison task that never rises above its 1.0% baseline through 2.5M training examples is major subtraction, specifically — major ranking climbs to 69.7% over the same range.
  3. Inverse search — going from an attribute back to the person — sits under 2% across every one of 320 ordinary pretraining-configuration × question-variant cells tested, recovering only when the training text is literally rewritten in reverse order. The paper attributes this to the left-to-right autoregressive factorization specifically, and the same pattern shows up qualitatively in GPT-3.5/GPT-4 across Jane Austen novels, Wikipedia bios, and two Chinese-language tasks.
